extracted.intended_audience: aspiring writers, literary readers, and contributors to periodicals
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and observations about literary composition, authorship conduct, and social performance of wit—aimed at those who write for or participate in the literary culture of periodical publications and salons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different skills for writing vs conversation
rubrics_metrics.description: “A man may be very entertaining and instructive upon paper ... and exceedingly dull in common discourse.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that being a good writer does not guarantee engaging social conversation. Written work can marshal and arrange ideas in ways a spontaneous conversation cannot; conversely, conversational wit often relies on a small, easily managed stock of ideas that can be displayed quickly. Prepare and adapt content to the medium: what succeeds on the page may need different handling in person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manageability of ideas — quality over quantity
rubrics_metrics.description: “A small stock of ideas is more easily managed, and sooner displayed, than a great quantity crowded together.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize a concise, well-handled set of ideas rather than overwhelming the audience with many scattered thoughts. In both writing and conversation, clarity and manageability help the performer or author to appear more composed and effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid affectation as a route to humour
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of affected stuttering, assumed madness, feigned blindness, and other contrived defects are shown to produce laughs but are described as contrivances: the stutterer ‘extorted the laugh of the company' and an affectation can become habitual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affectation (pretending stammers, illnesses, or eccentricities) may momentarily amuse but is inauthentic and risks becoming a permanent, stigmatizing habit. Rely on genuine wit and invention rather than artificial quirks; affected performance is an anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: One wit at a time — avoid crowded cleverness
rubrics_metrics.description: “One wit, like a knuckle of ham in soup, gives a zest and flavour to the dish; but more than one serves only to spoil the pottage.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In gatherings or collaborative pieces, allow a single strong comic voice or brilliant turn to shine; too many competing wits dilute effect and create cacophony. Structure group conversation or multi-author work so strengths are highlighted rather than clashing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not obscure argument with pedantry
rubrics_metrics.description: The pedant who ‘involved himself in a cloud of Greek and Latin quotations, which nobody attempted to dispel’ produced a ‘confused hum of insipid observations’ and made the evening dull.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overloading readers or listeners with learned references or technical jargon that do not illuminate the point. Use erudition to clarify and support, not to dazzle or obscure; keep to the subject and make your examples relevant and comprehensible to the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use historically appropriate metrics when debating poetic form
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation that the ancients had neither blank verse nor rhyme, 'which were measured by feet, whereas ours are reckoned by the number of syllables.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When discussing or defending poetic forms, base arguments on accurate knowledge of metrics and historical practice. Do not misapply ancient authorities to modern forms without acknowledging differences in metrical systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity in praise vs the dangers of panegyric
rubrics_metrics.description: An author printed a panegyric as a mortifying device; panegyric is characterised as in effect 'a species of infamy' and may be used as social weaponry (Wyvil’s panegyrick/satire incident).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious about insincere praise: panegyric can be perceived as false and may provoke contempt or retaliation. Choose whether to praise or satirize with regard to honesty and consequences; insincere or manipulative praise is ethically and reputationally risky.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novels (as practical models): combine moral instruction with knowledge of character
rubrics_metrics.description: Female novelists are praised for publishing 'merely for the propagation of virtue, with so much ease and spirit, and delicacy, and knowledge of the human heart,' enchanting and reforming readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For fiction aimed at broad readerships, combine engaging narrative and style with moral or emotional insight into human character. Moral purpose, elegance of style, and psychological knowledge are qualities the author applauds in successful novel-writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors and critics must expect backlash from censure
rubrics_metrics.description: The proprietor 'directs a literary journal, in which their productions are necessarily brought to trial' and even slight censure 'has rankled in the hearts of those authors' provoking anonymous libels and lampoons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you act as editor or critic, maintain candour and impartiality but be aware that critique—even fair ones—may provoke envy and retaliatory attacks. Weigh the duty to honest judgment against the social consequences, and prepare for personal or professional pushback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hosts/gatherings of authors should provide focal entertainment
rubrics_metrics.description: As they are afraid of making free with one another, 'they should bring each his butt, or whet-stone, along with him, for the entertainment of the company.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When organizing literary gatherings, provide or solicit material or activities that encourage free exchange and avoid stilted, jealous silence. Structure the event to prompt contributions so conversation does not stagnate through mutual reserve.
